{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the belly line (stroke 2), the full lower outline of the fish, and it came out clean and continuous. I also took ownership of the nose joint, the point where the start domino hands the fall to the top line. I inspected it closely, found the cause (a jammed domino and a sideways offset just past the nose), and bridged it. After that, about 108 of the 111 standing dominoes were connected to the start. The three that weren't were strays by the nose that don't affect the outline. The fish has a clear body and tail, so the judge should recognise it.

Execution: I laid the belly in several passes straight from Sofia's sketch. I then used close inspections to find where the chain was actually breaking, instead of guessing. I fixed the break with targeted bridging and by clearing the jammed domino, rather than re-laying the whole line. I confirmed the result by tracing the fall by eye before calling it done.

Collaboration: I told the table where I was working and what I was doing at the nose, so Sofia and Jack could keep clear of it and nobody bumped anyone else's work. I asked Jack to check the tail join and Sofia to check the middle crossing, so each of us owned a different part of the fish. I also said plainly when the top line was still pale, so the team could focus on it.

Leadership: Near the end I called for hands-off. I asked for a final look at the middle and tail and said that anyone who saw a pale stretch should point at it. That kept the table from adding risk to a fish that was already standing, and it stood through to the push. I think my part, the belly and the nose connection, was a central piece of the result, though the table delivered it together.", "my_share_percent": 30}
